xray.one_line: A general AI agent that plans and carries out tasks on its own cloud computer, browsing, running code and acting in the apps you connect.
xray.what_it_does: Manus is an autonomous general AI agent that completes tasks rather than answering questions: it works in a sandbox virtual computer with internet access, a persistent file system and the ability to install software, and can keep a persistent Cloud Computer running 24/7. Its 416 connectors let it read data from and take actions in services such as Gmail, Notion, Slack and GitHub, while Browser Operator and Manus Studio extend it to the user's own logged-in browser and computer. Automations let it start work on a schedule or on an event in a connected app, without the user opening a task. [s4, s14, s9, s5, s8, s21]

situations.title: SilentBridge: a page summary that reached Gmail (2025)
reach: Untrusted content the agent reads while working: web pages, search results and documents, including hidden instructions in them
The user's Gmail, through Manus's first-party email connector
Code and shell execution inside the agent's sandbox, where passwordless sudo gave root
The agent's own deploy_expose_port tool, which could publish its internal code server to the internet
Secrets in the agent container: API keys and internal endpoints in environment variables
Outbound network to any server, including one the attacker controls
asked_our_example: Summarise the page or document the user pointed to, and nothing else
Use the Gmail connector only for a request about the user's own email
gap: Content the agent was only meant to read could drive connector calls and outbound requests: the research found no separation between information to summarise and instructions to execute, and no per-operation consent for connector actions.

The sandbox was over-privileged: code execution by default, passwordless sudo, secrets in the environment and a tool that exposes internal services, so one injected instruction reached root and the platform's own credentials.

situations.title: September 2026: one email to code execution
reach: Incoming email the agent reads through the Gmail connector, including hidden instructions in it
The agent's server-side JavaScript runtime, where decoded content was executed
A reverse shell inside the app, opened through a remote code execution bug
Credentials and tokens for the accounts the victim had linked, which could include Gmail, Dropbox or GitHub
Manus's prompt-injection check, which spots a prompt hidden in data and notifies the owner
asked_our_example: Read and process the user's email as data
Run code only when the user's own request calls for it
gap: Email content could become executable code in the agent's runtime: the check flagged plain injected commands but warned only after an obfuscated payload had already run.
From the runtime, the tokens of every linked account were within reach, so one email reached every service the user had connected.

situations.title: Browser Operator inside your logged-in browser
reach: The user's local desktop browser, its existing logins and active tabs, from the user's own IP address
Messages and posting on the user's social accounts, such as LinkedIn messages and Twitter posts
Job application sites, submitting applications with the user's attached resume
Shopping accounts, such as the user's Amazon order history
Accounts the user logs into in the Cloud Browser: email, CRM, social media, premium research tools
asked_our_example: Read unread LinkedIn messages and draft replies to job offers; send nothing
Work only on the site named in the task
gap: Authorisation is documented per session, not per site or per action: once granted, the agent works with every login in the browser, and nothing documented makes a session read-only.
Actions come from the user's own browser and IP, which the vendor says sites see as genuine, so the sites' own controls cannot tell the agent from the person.

questions: When a task has read untrusted content (a page, a document or an email), can connector calls, code execution and outbound requests be made to wait for the user's approval, as Automations' Approval required does for sends?
Can a Browser Operator session be limited to one site, or to read-only, rather than covering every login in the browser, and can the action log be exported?
After SilentBridge and the Salt Labs finding, can code the agent runs still reach the tokens of connected accounts, and is passwordless sudo still the sandbox default?
Cue agents have their own email, phone number and wallet and pay within a budget the user sets: who can change that budget, and is each payment recorded against a named person?
Since the separation from Meta, which entity processes customer and connector data, under which jurisdiction, and are the published SOC 2 and ISO attestations for that entity?
incidents: 2025-08: Embrace The Red showed an indirect prompt injection in a PDF making Manus call its deploy_expose_port tool without a human in the loop, expose its internal VS Code Server to the internet and leak the URL and password to a third party, giving full control of the agent's dev box. Disclosed to Manus on 1 June 2025; the author said the status of mitigations remained unclear at publication. [s40]

2026-02: Aurascape AuraLabs published SilentBridge, zero-click indirect prompt injection through web pages, search results and documents (each scored CVSS 9.8), demonstrating Gmail exfiltration, secret extraction, a root shell in the sandbox, public exposure of the internal code server and unauthenticated access to other customers' media on a public CDN. Found September 2025; Manus mitigated in November 2025. [s35, s36]

2026-09: Salt Labs turned one email into remote code execution in Manus: a JSFuck-obfuscated payload ran before the prompt-injection check warned, and a reverse shell exposed tokens for connected accounts such as Gmail, Dropbox or GitHub. Disclosed through Meta's bug bounty programme and patched. [s37, s38, s39]

help.pitch: RiskMandate would measure, for one real deployment of Manus's agents, what each agent was asked to do (its mandate), what its credentials and connections actually let it reach (its grant), and the difference between the two (the gap), and keep that as a written record. It is read-only: never in the request path.
